extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, communications/PR students, and organizational communications staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on managing relationships between organizations and news media — when and how to provide information (press releases, media lists, information subsidies) and ethical/practical standards for doing so. Covers aims, tactics, journalist expectations, and ethical pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of media relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Involves working with media for the purpose of informing the public of an organization's mission, policies and practices in a positive, consistent and credible manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goal is to maximize positive coverage in the mass media without paying for it directly through advertising; can also develop symbiotic relationships with media outlets, journalists, bloggers, and influencers to garner publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate media relations from public relations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Media relations" refers to the relationship that a company or organization develops with journalists, whereas "public relations" extends that relationship beyond the media to the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand scope: media relations is one component of broader PR and of integrated marketing communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know journalists' beats and areas of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to ensure a positive working relationship with media personnel is to become deeply familiar with their "beats" and areas of interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor pitches and materials to what specific journalists and outlets cover; relevancy to a beat increases chances of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and use a media list
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations often compile what is known as a media list, or a list of possible media outlets who may be interested in an organization's information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the media landscape is large, a media list assists in determining which outlet may be most interested in a particular story when a newsworthy event occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select outreach occasions based on newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible reasons an organization may reach out to the media include launch of a new product/service; initiation of new factories/offices; financial results; organization-sponsored events or awards; launch of promotional campaigns; recent disasters, strikes or organizational closures; awards/accolades; visits from dignitaries/celebrities; involvement in local/community activities; community engagement; providing a point of view on a negative news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these types of events as triggers for media outreach; ensure the event is genuinely newsworthy for the targeted outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide information subsidies (ready-to-publish material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information subsidy consists of information that is provided to the press as supplemental material to help present their reporting. This includes information such as press releases, advertisements, and videos of related news events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: can decrease or eliminate the need for completing additional research by media and save journalists time/money. But journalists vet sources for accuracy and bias; not all subsidies will be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure accuracy and minimize bias in materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust in the source and content of the data are the criteria journalists use when determining whether or not they will use the material provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because subsidies present ready-to-publish data, practitioners must ensure factual accuracy and be transparent about potential bias to maintain credibility with journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay up to date on relevant news and current events
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners expand their client's media coverage by staying up to date on news and current events that are relevant to their client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being informed helps practitioners identify story angles and timely opportunities for pitching; it also helps maintain credibility as a reliable source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build and maintain trust in relationships with journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust is a critical component between the media and PR practitioners and it must be present for there to be a successful working relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both parties should be committed to working together; practitioners should provide newsworthy, reliable information to sustain trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid embellishing or misrepresenting facts (ethical honesty)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is now more important than ever for public relations practitioners to provide honest, truthful, and accurate information to the media. There is much pressure for a public relations practitioner to embellish the truth for their client to make news appear better than it really is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should authenticate information they receive; practitioners should resist embellishment and provide more detail rather than spin when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be upfront about potential ethical issues
rubrics_metrics.description: One way a PR practitioner can avoid ethical issues is to be upfront with their clients and the media regarding any potential ethical issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a basis for personal and professional ethics that considers the interests of self, the media, and the entity represented; include respect and social responsibility as core principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a virtue-based approach to ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Another approach to ethics is based on virtue. This includes learning from others, being prepared to take risks, and practicing complete honesty in their reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate professional virtues (honesty, learning, responsible risk-taking) as part of ethical media relations practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits: media cannot be controlled
rubrics_metrics.description: Dealing with the media presents unique challenges in that the news media cannot be controlled — they have ultimate control over whether stories pitched to them are of interest to their audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on building relationships and providing relevant, accurate material rather than attempting to control coverage; accept that editors/journalists make final decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand practitioners' perceived bias and address it
rubrics_metrics.description: Because PR practitioners are usually focused on a client, some would argue that they are biased or attempt to sway public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge potential perceptions of bias; improve the type and quality of news data provided in response to journalist feedback to strengthen the working relationship.
